title: Factors, Common Factors & HCF
summary: One lesson for Set 6 after listing common multiples: list the factors of a number (using the calculator to test each divisor), find common factors by listing, and pick out the HCF. Scaffolding is weaned off through each set; all questions are authored by hand.

els.text: Factors, Common Factors & HCF
Test with the calculator. List in order.
KEY DEFINITION
Factor

A factor of a number divides into it exactly, with no remainder.

Factors come in pairs: $3 \times 8 = 24$, so $3$ and $8$ are both factors of $24$.

$1$ and the number itself are always factors.

slides.title: Testing a factor with the calculator
slides.brief: Type the sum exactly as shown. The fx-85 shows a non-whole answer as a fraction; S⇔D swaps it to a decimal. Build up with each click.

els.text: Testing a factor with the calculator
Is $4$ a factor of $24$? Is $5$?
A whole number: $4$ is a factor of $24$ (and so is $6$).
S⇔D
Not a whole number: $5$ is not a factor of $24$.
Whole number: it is a factor. Fraction or decimal: it is not.

slides.title: Finding all the factors of 24

els.text: Finding all the factors of 24
Stop when the answer is smaller than the number you divided by.
$4.8$ is smaller than $5$, so stop. Factors of $24$: $1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 12, 24$

slides.brief: Pupils type 24 ÷ 1, 24 ÷ 2, ... and fill the rows. Stop at 5: the answer is smaller than 5. If the class is quick, check the replay key on the fx-85GT CW to change the divisor without retyping.

items.title: Factors of $48$
question: List all the factors of $48$.
$1 \times 48,\;\;2 \times 24$
$3 \times \square,\;\;4 \times 12$
$6 \times \square$
explanation: $48 \div 5 = 9.6$ is not a whole number, so $5$ is not a factor.
items.rationale: Divide by 1, 2, 3, ... in order, keep each exact pair and stop when the answer is smaller than the divisor.

els.text: KEY DEFINITION
Common factor
A common factor of two numbers is a number that is a factor of both.

slides.title: Find the common factors
slides.brief: List the smaller number's factors with the calculator, then test each one on the bigger number. Circle the numbers in both lists.

els.text: Find the common factors
List the factors of both numbers. Which are in both lists?
Common factors: $1$, $2$, $3$, $6$
Calculator check: is $4$ a factor of $18$? $18 \div 4 = 4.5$. No, so $4$ is not a common factor.

slides.title: Discuss

els.text: DISCUSS
Kofi says: "The only common factor of $12$ and $18$ is $6$." Is he right?
KEY POINT
No. $1$, $2$ and $3$ are common factors too. $1$ is a factor of every number.
QUESTION
Do $8$ and $9$ have a common factor? How do you know?
ANSWER
Yes: $1$. The factors of $8$ are $1, 2, 4, 8$ and of $9$ are $1, 3, 9$. Only $1$ is in both.

slides.brief: Short discussion after the 12 and 18 model. Pupils meet the idea that two numbers can have several common factors, and that 1 is always one of them.

slides.title: Highest common factor (HCF)
slides.brief: Reuse the 12 and 18 lists from the common factors slide: circle the common factors, then pick the highest.

els.text: KEY DEFINITION
Highest common factor (HCF)
The HCF of two numbers is the largest number that is a factor of both.
Common factors: $1$, $2$, $3$, $6$
The highest is $6$, so the HCF of $12$ and $18$ is $6$.

slides.title: Discuss

els.text: DISCUSS
Ruby says: "The HCF of $12$ and $18$ is $36$." What has she found?
KEY POINT
$36$ is in the $12$ and $18$ times tables, so it is a common multiple, not a common factor.
QUESTION
Can the HCF of $12$ and $18$ ever be bigger than $12$? Why not?
ANSWER
No. A factor of $12$ is never bigger than $12$, so the HCF cannot be more than $12$.

slides.brief: Separates the HCF from the common multiples of last lesson: 36 is the first common multiple of 12 and 18.
